Polissia Wetland Map

BogSignal · Polissia, 2026

Where the wetlands of Polissia are

Each coloured dot is a place our model reads as wetland, open water or peat soil. Green is living wetland. Orange is peat that is now farmed.

Show
Zoom
  • Wetland

    Swamp (wet forest) and marsh (wet grass and reeds). The places still working as wetland.

  • Open water

    Lakes, rivers, reservoirs and ponds.

  • Farmed peat

    Peat soil now used as cropland. Usually drained wetland.

  • Other peat land

    Peat soil under forest, meadow or shrub, not farmed and not mapped as wetland.

Polissia region, approximate outline

Areas are estimates for the mapped part of the region, rounded to 100 km².

The model analysed about 133,000 km², 74% of the study area; the rest lacked complete satellite coverage. Each dot on the whole-region view covers about 340 m; the model itself works at 20 m.

How well it finds wetlands: the ensemble results

Our best result averages six models, three U-Nets and three TerraMind models, all reading the three sensors together. On an area held back from training it does clearly better than any single model.

What NISAR adds is not settled. Using all three sensors beat Sentinel-2 + Sentinel-1 by 5.4 points on the test area, but across five geographic folds the difference averaged −2.1 points, ranging from −9.0 to +10.2.

The map above is drawn from a single all-sensor U-Net (model D), not from the ensemble. All scores measure agreement with existing reference maps, not with ground checks. Source: the team's model experiments report on the ensemble branch.

How to read it

Switch to “Existing reference maps” to see what older maps show. Where the two views agree, the model is repeating what was already known. Where the model adds green, it is suggesting places worth a closer look.

The model's map is a guide for where to look, not a confirmed survey. Nobody has checked these places on the ground.

DataWhat it isWhat we used it for
NISAR GCOV (NASA and ISRO)L-band radar brightness, HH and HV, from ascending and descending passesModel input. Longer radar waves reach under vegetation

Satellite data were accessed through the Alaska Satellite Facility (NISAR) and Google Earth Engine (Sentinel). The model is a U-Net that reads all three sensors together and labels every 20 m pixel.
